title: Residential demand turn-up
dek: Experiments that paid households with free electricity may reveal whether flexible demand can become durable grid infrastructure rather than a clever trial.
whyTracked: The study offers a quantitative baseline with direct policy relevance and several observable routes to peer review, replication, regulation, and operational deployment.

current.assessment: The randomized trials are promising but remain a working-paper result tied to two European markets and a shared research lineage.
current.nextReviewTrigger: Review for a revised or peer-reviewed paper, independent replication, regulatory adoption, or utility-scale results with equity and curtailment measures.

openQuestions: Will peer review materially change the estimates or interpretation?
Can automated, local demand turn-up reduce actual curtailment at scale without burdening or excluding households?
Who captures the welfare gains under different tariff and compensation rules?

watchFor.trigger: The paper is published, revised, critiqued, or independently replicated.

watchFor.description: Operational rollout with measured curtailment outcomes
watchFor.trigger: A utility or system operator reports program-scale energy, equity, and grid results.
A jurisdiction changes tariffs or market rules to support demand turn-up.

observations.headline: Point-zero observation
observations.summary: Randomized residential trials reported that temporary discounts and free electricity increased consumption during renewable-abundance windows, while paying customers beyond a zero price added little further response.

sources.title: A Demand-Side Alternative to Renewable Curtailment
